title: Bhishma's Passing in Krishna's Presence
story:
Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows and would not die until the sky gave him his hour.

He had fallen in the war he had foreseen and refused to leave, holding his life in his hands through the last of the fighting, waiting for the sun to enter the northern course — the auspicious solstice on which those who give up the body pass to what does not pass away. The war ended. The field fell silent. The survivors came and sat by him, and still he waited, and taught, and watched the sky.

Then Krishna came to the field, and the sight of him walking toward the bed of arrows undid something in the old warrior that the arrows had never touched. "See," Bhishma said to the kings around him, "the compassion of the Lord toward his unalloyed devotees. This very Krishna has come to me as I give up my life, out of love for those who love him without reserve. May he be my refuge." And he asked one thing only: "Merging my mind in him with devotion, chanting his name with my voice, may that God of gods, the Lord, wait until I give up this body."

So Krishna stood before him, and Bhishma, with the Pandavas and the gathered sages looking on, gave what remained of his strength to the teaching he had carried all his life — the duties of charity and of kings, the duties of those who seek release, and the four ends of a human life, each in its place, each with its means, spoken according to the rank and stage of the one who heard it. He spoke of dharma the way a man speaks who is about to leave it behind, and while he spoke, the hour he had waited for came and stood at his shoulder.

Then Bhishma gathered in his speech and let the words go. He fixed his unblinking gaze upon the four-armed Krishna standing before him in yellow robes, and his last prayer went up like a flame finding the sky: "May my love rest on Krishna —" and the praise poured out of him, the long remembrance of a lifetime of watching.

He remembered Krishna dark as the tamala tree, his garments bright as the rays of the sun, driving the chariot through the dust of the battlefield with his locks disheveled and sweat on his face. He remembered how, at the height of the war, Krishna had placed the chariot between the two armies; how, hearing his friend's plea, he had set aside his own word and leapt down from the chariot — Krishna, who had sworn he would not fight — striding out to make true the vow of the old warrior who had pressed him to it, his armor shattered by sharp arrows, bathed in blood, glorious to behold. He remembered the great assembly at Yudhishthira's Rajasuya, crowded with sages and kings, where the same Lord had moved among them with his gentle smile and his loving glance. And at the end of the remembering: "Him, the unborn, dwelling in the heart of every embodied being — on him let my love rest."

The gaze did not waver. With pure concentration, his mind freed from attachment and fixed on the Primal Person, his sins burned away by that one sight, the weariness of a hundred wounds fell from him as a garment falls — gone, as the old tellers would say, by the very look of the Lord.

And when the sages around him knew that Bhishma was merging into the attributeless Brahman, the drums sounded — played by gods and men together, a roll of thunder over the field where he lay. The rites for the departed were performed, and the old warrior who had waited so long for his hour passed from the field, his mind in Krishna and Krishna's name on his lips, into the silence from which no one returns.
reflection: Bhishma's death completes his life's discipline: the man who spent his strength in waiting spends his last hour in praise, and the gaze he fixes on Krishna does what no art could — the weariness of the war falls from him by that sight alone. He does not cling to life; he looks at the Lord, and the looking is the release.
next_story_tease: That field would be remembered for the trembling of the earth beneath the gathered armies.
